title: Batch ETL Foundations: ShopFlow Orders Pipeline
tagline: Turn messy raw CSV and JSON exports into clean, query-ready analytics tables you can trust.
summary: You'll build a re-runnable batch ETL pipeline in Python that ingests ShopFlow's raw order, customer, product, order-item, and clickstream exports, validates and cleans them, and loads modeled analytics tables into a local DuckDB warehouse. Along the way you'll handle the real-world mess of production data — nulls, duplicates, wrong types, and broken foreign keys — and finish with automated data-quality checks and sample business queries. This is the foundation the next four projects build on, so you'll establish clean datasets and conventions the whole ladder reuses.
scenario: ShopFlow is a growing e-commerce company whose operational data lives in a transactional database and a clickstream tracker, both of which dump nightly exports to a shared folder: CSV files for orders, customers, products, and order_items, plus newline-delimited JSON for clickstream events. The analytics team currently opens these in spreadsheets by hand, which is slow, error-prone, and impossible to trust. As the company's first data engineer, you're asked to replace the manual process with an automated batch pipeline that reliably lands clean, deduplicated, well-typed tables in an analytical store so analysts can answer questions like daily revenue and top products without wrangling raw files.
learningGoals: Extract structured data from CSV and newline-delimited JSON files into Python data frames
Profile raw data to discover nulls, duplicates, type inconsistencies, and referential-integrity gaps
Design and apply an explicit schema with type coercion and safe null handling
Enforce referential integrity between fact and dimension tables during cleaning
Model raw sources into clean analytics tables (dimensions and facts) in DuckDB
Make loads idempotent so the pipeline can be re-run safely without duplicating data
Write lightweight data-quality assertions that fail loudly when expectations are violated
Answer real business questions with SQL against the loaded warehouse
skillsDemonstrated: Built an end-to-end batch ETL pipeline in Python (pandas) landing data in DuckDB
Implemented schema validation, type coercion, and null-handling for heterogeneous CSV/JSON sources
Enforced referential integrity and deduplication across fact and dimension tables
Designed idempotent, re-runnable load logic using upsert/merge and staging patterns
Authored automated data-quality assertions to gate pipeline output
Modeled a star-schema-friendly analytics layer and wrote analytical SQL
Structured a reproducible data project with configuration, logging, and tests
prerequisites: Comfortable writing basic Python (functions, loops, dictionaries, reading files)
Familiarity with the command line and running scripts
Basic SQL: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOIN
A working Python environment with pip or uv/venv
Understanding of what CSV and JSON files look like
datasetDescription: You start from ShopFlow's nightly raw exports in a data/raw/ folder. orders.csv: order_id (string), customer_id (string), order_ts (mixed date formats), status (e.g. placed/shipped/cancelled), order_total (string with occasional currency symbols) — contains some duplicate rows and null customer_ids. customers.csv: customer_id, email, full_name, country, signup_date — has duplicate customer_ids and inconsistent country casing. products.csv: product_id, product_name, category, unit_price, is_active — some unit_price values are blank. order_items.csv: order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, item_price — includes rows referencing order_ids or product_ids that do not exist (orphan rows). events.jsonl: newline-delimited JSON clickstream with event_id, session_id, customer_id (sometimes null for anonymous users), event_type (view/add_to_cart/checkout), product_id, event_ts — includes malformed/partial records. A data/raw/README describes each field.
architectureFlow: Raw exports (orders.csv, customers.csv, products.csv, order_items.csv, events.jsonl) -> Extract (Python readers) -> Profile (null/dupe/type report) -> Validate & Clean (schema coercion, null handling, dedup, referential integrity) -> Stage (Parquet in data/staging) -> Transform & Model (dim_customers, dim_products, fct_orders, fct_order_items, fct_events) -> Idempotent Load (DuckDB upsert/merge) -> Data-Quality Checks (assertions) -> Analytics tables (DuckDB) -> Sample SQL queries (daily revenue, top products)

title: Analytics Warehouse with dbt
tagline: Turn ShopFlow's raw loaded tables into a tested, documented dimensional model using dbt
summary: Building on the raw ShopFlow tables landed by your Project 1 batch ETL, you will construct a layered analytics engineering project with dbt. You will declare sources over the raw schema, build a clean staging layer that renames and casts columns, add intermediate models that join and deduplicate, and publish marts as a proper dimensional model (fct_orders, dim_customers, dim_products). Along the way you will add data tests and contracts, convert a growing fact table to an incremental model that safely handles late-arriving events, write documentation with descriptions and an exposure, build an aggregate metrics mart, and wire dbt build into a CI-style workflow. The result is a warehouse that analysts can trust and query.
scenario: ShopFlow's Project 1 pipeline reliably lands raw customers, orders, order_items, and products tables into the warehouse's raw schema every night, but analysts are writing brittle, duplicated SQL against those raw tables and getting different numbers for the same metric. The head of analytics asks you to create a single source of truth: cleaned, conformed, well-named models with documented business logic and automated tests, so that 'revenue last month' and 'active customers' mean the same thing to everyone. You adopt dbt to version-control transformations, enforce a staging-to-marts layering convention, and ship a dimensional model plus a metrics mart that powers the BI dashboards.
learningGoals: Structure a dbt project into sources, staging, intermediate, and marts layers with clear naming conventions
Choose and configure materializations (view, table, ephemeral, incremental) based on model role and cost
Design a star schema with fact and dimension tables and conformed grain
Write and run dbt tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values) plus enforce a model contract
Build an incremental model with unique_key and is_incremental() that correctly handles late-arriving data
Generate and serve dbt docs, define an exposure, and produce an aggregate metrics mart
Run dbt build in a reproducible CI-style workflow so every change is tested before merge

CI automation for data transformations (dbt build)

Python 3.9+ and pip for installing dbt

datasetDescription: The raw ShopFlow e-commerce tables produced by Project 1, living in a raw (or landing) schema: raw.customers (customer_id, name, email, signup_ts, country, raw dumped from source with possible nulls and inconsistent casing), raw.orders (order_id, customer_id, order_ts, status, order_total, currency), raw.order_items (order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price), and raw.products (product_id, sku, name, category, price, is_active). The data contains realistic messiness: duplicate rows from re-runs, mixed-case emails, string dates needing casting, and occasional late-arriving orders inserted after the nightly load, which motivates deduplication, contracts, and incremental logic.
architectureFlow: Raw loaded tables -> dbt sources (source freshness) -> Staging models (clean/rename/cast, views) -> Intermediate models (joins/dedup, ephemeral) -> Marts: dim_customers + dim_products + fct_orders (incremental) + agg metrics -> Tests + Contracts + Docs/Exposures -> BI dashboards & ad-hoc queries

tagline: Turn your batch ETL and dbt models into a scheduled, self-healing production pipeline
summary: In Projects 1 and 2 you built a batch ETL job and a dbt warehouse for ShopFlow, but both still run when you type a command by hand. title: Real-Time Streaming for ShopFlow with Kafka + Spark Structured Streaming
tagline: Turn ShopFlow's clickstream and orders into second-by-second metrics with exactly-once guarantees.
summary: You will stand up a local streaming platform alongside ShopFlow's existing batch stack. Using Docker Compose you run a single-broker Kafka cluster, write a Python producer that emits realistic clickstream and order events, and consume them with Spark Structured Streaming. Along the way you handle Avro/JSON deserialization against a schema, compute event-time windowed aggregations with watermarks to tolerate late-arriving events, maintain stateful counters, and achieve exactly-once delivery through checkpointing plus an idempotent sink. You finish by serving live metrics to a query-able store and a dashboard, tuning throughput and backpressure, and reconciling the streaming numbers against the batch warehouse from Projects 1-2 (the lambda/kappa question). The result is a production-shaped real-time pipeline you can demo end to end.
scenario: ShopFlow's growth team is tired of waiting until the next morning's batch load to see how a flash sale is performing. When a promotion goes live, they want live GMV, orders-per-minute, top categories, and add-to-cart-to-purchase conversion updating within seconds, not hours. The batch platform you built in Projects 1-3 stays as the source of truth for finance, but marketing and on-call engineers need a real-time view to react during traffic spikes and to catch payment failures as they happen. Your job is to build the streaming layer: ingest ShopFlow's clickstream and order events off Kafka, compute rolling windowed metrics that stay correct even when mobile events arrive minutes late, guarantee no double-counting during restarts, and publish the results to a store the dashboard and alerting can read. milestones.deliverable: A running Compose stack plus a configurable producer that streams realistic ShopFlow clickstream and order events to Kafka, demonstrated with a consumer capture.

milestones.title: Read and Parse the Stream in Spark Structured Streaming
milestones.goal: Consume both Kafka topics from Spark Structured Streaming, deserialize against the schema, and produce a clean typed streaming DataFrame with proper event-time columns.
tasks: Create a Spark session configured with the Kafka and Avro packages and connect to the broker as a streaming source.
Subscribe to shopflow.clickstream and shopflow.orders and extract key, value, topic, partition, and offset.
Deserialize the value from Avro/JSON using the registered schema into typed columns.
Cast event_time from epoch millis to a proper Spark timestamp column for later event-time processing.
Filter or route malformed records to a dead-letter path instead of failing the whole batch.
Write the parsed stream to console sink to validate parsing before adding aggregations.
acceptanceCriteria: A running streaming query prints deserialized, correctly typed rows for both topics to the console.
event_time appears as a Spark TimestampType column, not a raw long, and matches the producer's timestamps.
Malformed or unparseable records are diverted to a dead-letter sink rather than crashing the query.
The query reports steady input rows/sec in the Spark UI matching the producer throughput.
hints: Use spark-submit --packages org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10 (and the Avro package) so the connectors are on the classpath.
from_avro / from_json turns the binary Kafka value into a struct you can select fields from.
startingOffsets='latest' during development avoids replaying the whole topic every run; switch to 'earliest' when testing recovery.
milestones.deliverable: A PySpark streaming job (read_parse.py) that reliably reads and parses both ShopFlow topics into typed DataFrames with a validated event-time column.

milestones.title: Event-Time Windows and Watermarks for Late Data
milestones.goal: Compute rolling windowed metrics on event time and add watermarks so late-arriving events are handled correctly and old state is dropped.
tasks: Apply a watermark on event_time (e.g. 5 minutes) to bound how late events can still be accepted.
Compute tumbling 1-minute windows for orders-per-minute and GMV, and a sliding window for top categories.
Group by window plus dimension (category, device) and aggregate counts and sums.
Deliberately inject events late (within and beyond the watermark) and observe which update their window and which are dropped.
Compare tumbling vs sliding window results and document the tradeoff in latency vs smoothness.
Choose an output mode (update/append) appropriate for windowed aggregation and justify it.
acceptanceCriteria: Windowed aggregates are keyed by event_time windows, not processing time, and results shift when producer clock skew is introduced.
Late events within the watermark correctly update their original window; events beyond it are dropped as expected.
The chosen watermark and output mode are documented with the reasoning for the values selected.
GMV and orders-per-minute windows sum to the same totals as a manual count of produced events over the same interval.
hints: withWatermark must be applied before the windowed groupBy or Spark ignores it.
Append output mode only emits a window once it closes (after the watermark passes), which delays results but is safe for downstream idempotent writes.
To see late-data behavior clearly, run the producer with a high late-event fraction and log the min/max event_time per micro-batch.
milestones.deliverable: A windowed aggregation job (windowed_metrics.py) with watermarks that produces correct event-time metrics and a short write-up of the late-data and window-type tradeoffs.

milestones.title: Stateful Aggregation with an Exactly-Once Idempotent Sink
milestones.goal: Maintain cross-batch state and write results to a serving store with exactly-once guarantees using checkpointing plus an idempotent or transactional sink.
tasks: Add stateful aggregation such as running per-session conversion (add_to_cart to paid) using flatMapGroupsWithState or windowed state.
Configure a checkpoint location so offsets and state persist across restarts.
Implement the sink with foreachBatch that writes to Postgres/Delta using an idempotent upsert keyed by window+dimension (or batchId dedupe).
Ensure the write and offset commit cannot double-apply: use MERGE/ON CONFLICT or a transactional write with the batch id.
Send deliberate duplicate events from the producer and confirm the sink totals are not inflated.
Document why at-least-once source + idempotent sink yields effective exactly-once end to end.
acceptanceCriteria: The serving store contains windowed metrics that update correctly across multiple micro-batches without duplicates.
Injecting duplicate source events does not change the aggregated totals in the sink.
Re-running the same batch (or replaying offsets) produces identical sink state, proving idempotency.
Checkpoint directory contains committed offsets and state, and the job resumes from it rather than reprocessing everything.
The exactly-once reasoning (source semantics + idempotent sink) is documented in recovery_notes.md.
hints: foreachBatch gives you a normal batch DataFrame per micro-batch, so you can do a transactional upsert your source connector wouldn't support directly.
Key the upsert on the natural window+dimension key so a replayed batch overwrites rather than appends.
Delta Lake's MERGE or Postgres INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE are the two cleanest idempotent-sink patterns.
milestones.deliverable: A stateful streaming job writing to a serving store via an idempotent exactly-once sink (exactly_once_sink.py), demonstrated to be duplicate-proof.

milestones.title: Fault Tolerance: Checkpoint Recovery and Late-Data Resilience
milestones.goal: Prove the pipeline survives failures by killing and restarting the job and confirming no data loss or duplication, and validate correct behavior under sustained late data.
tasks: While the producer runs, kill the Spark streaming job mid-batch and restart it from the same checkpoint.
Verify the job resumes from committed offsets and that sink totals remain correct after recovery.
Simulate a Kafka broker restart and confirm the consumer reconnects and continues without gaps.
Run a sustained burst of late events and confirm windows and watermark behave as designed.
Test a schema-evolution scenario (add an optional field) and confirm old and new events both parse.
Record recovery time, offset behavior, and any duplicates observed in recovery_notes.md.
acceptanceCriteria: After a kill-and-restart, the sink shows no missing or duplicated windows compared to a continuously-running baseline.
The restarted job logs resuming from the checkpoint's committed offsets, not from earliest.
A broker restart causes a temporary pause but the pipeline self-recovers and catches up.
The schema-evolution change does not break parsing of previously-produced events.
recovery_notes.md documents the failure scenarios tested and the observed outcomes.
hints: Compare the recovered run's sink to a golden run by producing a fixed, bounded set of events with a known expected total.
Do not delete the checkpoint between runs when testing recovery, that is what makes resume possible.
Making new schema fields optional with defaults keeps old messages readable and is the safest evolution path.
milestones.deliverable: A documented fault-tolerance test suite showing checkpoint-based recovery with zero loss/duplication plus late-data and schema-evolution resilience results.

milestones.title: Serving Layer, Throughput Tuning, and Batch Reconciliation
milestones.goal: Expose live metrics through a dashboard, tune the pipeline for throughput and backpressure, and reconcile streaming totals against the batch warehouse (the lambda/kappa question).
tasks: Design serving tables (real_time_gmv, orders_per_minute, category_leaderboard, session_conversion) and wire the sink to them.
Build a live dashboard (Grafana or Streamlit) reading the serving store with sub-minute refresh.
Ramp producer throughput and tune trigger interval, maxOffsetsPerTrigger, and shuffle partitions to sustain the load without growing lag.
Add monitoring: consumer lag, input rows/sec, batch duration, and state store size, with an alert threshold.
Write reconcile.py comparing a completed streaming window's GMV to the same interval in the dbt batch marts from Projects 1-2.
Document the lambda vs kappa tradeoff and how ShopFlow reconciles the fast (streaming) and slow (batch) paths.
Produce a short demo script that starts the stack, drives load, and shows the dashboard and reconciliation live.
acceptanceCriteria: The dashboard displays live GMV, orders-per-minute, top categories, and conversion, refreshing within a minute of events.
Under a throughput increase, tuning keeps consumer lag and batch duration bounded (documented before/after numbers).
Monitoring surfaces consumer lag, throughput, batch time, and state size, with a defined alert threshold.
reconcile.py shows streaming and batch GMV for the same interval agree within a small documented tolerance.
The README explains the lambda/kappa decision and how the streaming layer relates to the batch platform from earlier projects.
hints: maxOffsetsPerTrigger caps how much each micro-batch pulls, which is your main backpressure lever in Structured Streaming.
Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to roughly match your core count for streaming; the default 200 is usually far too high locally.
Reconcile only over closed windows (past the watermark) so late-data settling doesn't create false mismatches with batch.
milestones.deliverable: A live dashboard plus a tuned, monitored pipeline and a reconciliation report proving the streaming metrics agree with the batch warehouse, with a runnable end-to-end demo.

title: ShopFlow Cloud Lakehouse: The Unified Platform
tagline: Fuse your batch and streaming pipelines into one governed, cost-aware cloud lakehouse on S3 + Iceberg + Spark.
summary: This is the capstone of the ShopFlow ladder and the centerpiece of your data engineering portfolio. You will unify everything built in Projects 1-4 (batch ETL, a dbt warehouse, Airflow orchestration, and Kafka+Spark streaming) into a single cloud lakehouse. Object storage (S3) becomes the source of truth, an open table format (Apache Iceberg) delivers ACID transactions, time travel, and schema evolution, and Spark powers both batch and streaming writes into a medallion architecture (bronze -> silver -> gold). You will provision the whole stack with Terraform, orchestrate it with Airflow, wrap it in CI/CD with automated data tests, and finish with governance, lineage, PII controls, cost optimization, and end-to-end observability. The deliverable is a production-shaped platform plus an architecture diagram, a polished README, a recorded demo, and a cost/scale writeup that shows you can reason about a real system, not just a toy.
scenario: ShopFlow has outgrown its patchwork of pipelines. The batch ETL loads a nightly Postgres warehouse, dbt models live in a separate BigQuery-style warehouse, Airflow orchestrates some of it, and the new Kafka+Spark stream writes clickstream events to yet another store. Analysts complain that 'the numbers don't tie out', finance is alarmed at overlapping storage and compute bills, and the security team just flagged that raw customer PII is sitting unencrypted in three places. Leadership has approved a consolidation: build one cloud lakehouse where every dataset (orders, customers, products, inventory, and real-time clickstream) lands once in S3, is governed and versioned via Iceberg, is processed by Spark through a single medallion pipeline, and is served to BI from a shared gold layer. You are the platform engineer. Your mandate is to design, provision, and operate this lakehouse end-to-end, with the reliability, security, and cost discipline of a real production team.
learningGoals: Architect a cloud lakehouse that unifies batch and streaming ingestion on top of a single object-storage source of truth
Use an open table format (Apache Iceberg) to get ACID transactions, snapshot/time-travel queries, hidden partitioning, and safe schema evolution on S3
Implement a medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold) with clear contracts and quality gates between layers
Run Spark for both batch backfills and micro-batch streaming writes into the same lakehouse tables
Provision cloud infrastructure reproducibly with Terraform and manage environments (dev/prod) as code
Build CI/CD for data: linting, unit tests, dbt/data tests, and gated deploys of Spark jobs, dbt models, and DAGs
Apply governance in practice: a catalog, column/table-level access, data lineage, and PII masking/tokenization
Optimize cost and performance with file compaction, partition pruning, lifecycle policies, and right-sized compute
Instrument the platform with metrics, logs, freshness/SLA checks, and alerting so failures are caught before analysts notice
skillsDemonstrated: End-to-end cloud lakehouse design and delivery
Open table format engineering (Iceberg ACID, time travel, schema evolution, compaction)
Unified batch + streaming ingestion into shared tables
Spark batch and structured streaming on object storage
Infrastructure-as-code with Terraform (multi-environment)
CI/CD for data pipelines with automated data quality tests
Data governance: catalog, lineage, RBAC, and PII handling
Cost and performance optimization on a cloud data platform
Observability, SLAs, freshness monitoring, and alerting
Technical communication: architecture diagrams, README, and cost/scale writeups
techStack: AWS Glue Data Catalog (or Iceberg REST/Nessie catalog)
Apache Kafka / Amazon MSK (streaming source from Project 4)
Amazon Athena / Trino (SQL query + BI serving)
prerequisites: Completed Projects 1-4 of this ladder (batch ETL, dbt warehouse, Airflow orchestration, Kafka+Spark streaming), or equivalent experience
Comfortable writing PySpark transformations and reading Spark execution plans
Working knowledge of SQL and dbt models, tests, and sources
Basic AWS account access with permissions to create S3, IAM, Glue, and compute resources (a free-tier or low-budget account is fine)
Familiarity with Git, pull requests, and running CI in GitHub Actions
Understanding of Airflow DAGs, operators, and scheduling
Ability to read/write Terraform HCL at a basic level (variables, resources, modules)
A cost budget and awareness (set a billing alarm before you start; this project can incur real charges)
datasetDescription: You reuse the ShopFlow domain from earlier projects and consolidate all of it into the lakehouse. Batch sources: orders (order_id, customer_id, status, total_amount, currency, created_at, updated_at), customers (customer_id, email, full_name, phone, country, signup_date), products (product_id, category, price, cost, supplier_id), and inventory snapshots (product_id, warehouse_id, quantity_on_hand, snapshot_ts). These arrive as daily CSV/Parquet drops in a raw S3 prefix, mirroring the Project 1-3 extracts. Streaming source: the Project 4 clickstream topic on Kafka/MSK (event_id, session_id, customer_id, event_type, page, product_id, event_ts, user_agent) flowing continuously at hundreds to thousands of events per minute. Customers data contains PII (email, full_name, phone) that must be masked or tokenized before the silver layer. Volumes are portfolio-scale but realistic: tens of millions of historical order rows, low-tens-of-millions of daily clickstream events, so partitioning, compaction, and cost decisions genuinely matter. A small synthetic data generator (carried over/extended from earlier projects) can produce both the batch drops and the Kafka event stream so the platform can be demoed end-to-end without proprietary data.
architectureFlow: Batch drops (orders/customers/products/inventory) + Kafka clickstream (Project 4) -> S3 raw landing (object storage) -> Iceberg tables via Spark (bronze: batch backfill jobs + Spark Structured Streaming micro-batches) -> Spark silver (cleanse, conform, dedupe, PII mask, schema evolution) -> dbt gold marts on Iceberg -> Athena/Trino SQL + BI dashboards -> orchestrated by Airflow, deployed via Terraform + GitHub Actions CI/CD, governed by Glue catalog + OpenLineage lineage + RBAC, and monitored by CloudWatch/Grafana freshness & cost alerts

milestones.title: Provision the lakehouse foundation with Terraform
milestones.goal: Stand up all cloud infrastructure as code and create the empty Iceberg tables that will hold bronze/silver/gold data, so the entire platform is reproducible from a clean account.
tasks: Write Terraform modules for the S3 data lake (raw, bronze, silver, gold prefixes with versioning and default encryption), IAM roles/policies for Spark and Airflow, and the Glue Data Catalog database (or a Nessie/Iceberg REST catalog).

Configure the Iceberg catalog (warehouse location on S3, catalog type) and Spark's iceberg-spark-runtime + catalog settings in spark_jobs/conf.

Create initial Iceberg table DDL for bronze orders, customers, products, inventory, and clickstream, choosing partition specs (e.g. days(event_ts), category) and table properties (format-version=2, write.target-file-size-bytes).

milestones.title: Bronze ingestion: unify batch and streaming into Iceberg

tasks: Build a Spark batch job that reads the daily S3 raw drops (orders/customers/products/inventory), adds ingestion metadata (source_file, ingested_at, batch_id), and appends/merges into bronze Iceberg tables.
Build a Spark Structured Streaming job that consumes the Kafka/MSK clickstream, parses the event schema, and writes micro-batches into the bronze clickstream Iceberg table with checkpointing.
Implement idempotent ingestion so re-running a batch (same batch_id) or reprocessing a Kafka offset range does not create duplicates.
Add a maintenance step (or config) that keeps bronze file sizes reasonable, and verify hidden partitioning routes rows correctly.
Write a backfill path that can replay historical batch data into bronze from a given date, plus a small data generator invocation to produce demo volume.

Re-running a batch load produces no duplicate rows (idempotency proven with a row-count + primary-key check).
The streaming job recovers from a stop/restart using its checkpoint without data loss or duplication.
Bronze tables carry ingestion lineage columns (source, ingested_at, batch/offset) on every row.
A dated backfill command repopulates bronze correctly and completes within a documented time budget.

For streaming, foreachBatch + Iceberg append gives you exactly-once semantics when paired with checkpoint offsets.

milestones.deliverable: Working bronze ingestion (batch + streaming) writing to Iceberg, with idempotency and backfill demonstrated in the PR description.

milestones.title: Observability, docs, and portfolio packaging
milestones.goal: Operate the platform like a real team and package it as a portfolio centerpiece: metrics, freshness SLAs, alerting, an architecture diagram, a polished README, a recorded demo, and a cost/scale writeup.
tasks: Instrument metrics and logs (CloudWatch or Prometheus+Grafana): job success/failure, pipeline latency, streaming lag, row counts per layer, and data-freshness per gold table.
Define SLAs (e.g. gold facts fresh within N hours) and configure alerting (email/Slack) on failures, SLA misses, freshness breaches, and cost-anomaly thresholds.
Build one operational dashboard that shows platform health at a glance (pipeline runs, lag, freshness, cost trend).
Author docs: architecture.md with a clear diagram of the full flow, data_contracts.md, and a runbook covering common failures and recovery (including Iceberg snapshot rollback).
Write the README as the front door: problem, architecture diagram, how to deploy, how to run the demo, tech decisions and trade-offs, and a cost/scale section.
Record a 5-8 minute demo that walks batch + streaming data all the way to a dashboard, then triggers and recovers from a failure to show observability in action.
acceptanceCriteria: A health dashboard displays run status, streaming lag, per-layer row counts, and freshness for every gold table.
An injected failure (e.g. a bad batch or stalled stream) fires an alert within the defined SLA window.
The README lets a new reader understand the system and deploy the dev environment without asking questions.
The architecture diagram accurately depicts ingestion (batch+streaming) -> S3 -> Iceberg -> Spark -> medallion -> BI -> orchestration/CI-CD/observability.
A recorded demo shows end-to-end data flow plus a failure-and-recovery, and a cost/scale writeup discusses how the design scales 10x and where cost grows.
hints: Freshness (max event/updated timestamp vs now) is the single most convincing observability metric for a lakehouse.
In the demo, breaking something on purpose and showing the alert fire is more impressive than a happy path.
The cost/scale writeup is what separates a senior-looking portfolio from a bootcamp one; be specific with numbers and trade-offs.
milestones.deliverable: A health dashboard + alerting, complete docs (README, architecture diagram, contracts, runbook), a recorded demo, and a cost/scale writeup, packaged as the portfolio capstone.

productionChecklist: All infrastructure is defined in Terraform and reproducible in a clean account; no manual console changes drift from code
Bronze ingestion is idempotent for batch and exactly-once for streaming, with checkpoints and backfill paths proven
Silver and gold writes are gated by automated data tests (uniqueness, referential integrity, accepted values, freshness)
No raw PII exists beyond bronze; masking/tokenization is enforced and access to any reversible mapping is restricted and audited
Iceberg maintenance (compaction, snapshot expiration, orphan-file cleanup) runs on schedule to control file count and cost
S3 lifecycle policies tier or expire raw/low-value data, and compute is right-sized for the workload
CI runs lint + unit + data tests on every PR and blocks merge on failure; CD promotes to prod only after tests pass and approval
Column-level lineage is captured end-to-end and browsable from raw source to dashboard
Observability covers job status, latency, streaming lag, per-layer row counts, and per-table freshness, with alerting on SLA/freshness/cost breaches
A runbook documents recovery for common failures, including Iceberg snapshot rollback and streaming restart
Secrets and credentials are managed via a secrets store/IAM, never committed to the repo
The README, architecture diagram, and cost/scale writeup are complete and let a stranger deploy and understand the system
stretchGoals: Add change-data-capture (CDC) ingestion from a source database into bronze using Debezium + Kafka, upserting via Iceberg MERGE
Introduce catalog branching/tagging (Nessie or Iceberg branches) to run isolated 'write-audit-publish' deployments before promoting to main
Implement a real-time gold path: a low-latency streaming aggregation serving near-real-time metrics alongside the batch gold marts
Add automated data-quality anomaly detection (volume/nulls/distribution drift) that opens tickets instead of only alerting
Support multi-region or disaster-recovery with cross-region S3 replication and a failover runbook
Add a semantic layer / metrics store so BI definitions of 'revenue' are single-sourced and consistent across tools
Benchmark Iceberg vs Delta Lake on the same workload and document the trade-offs you observed
Introduce cost showback per data domain using resource tags and query-scan attribution
portfolioTips: This is the project you lead your resume and interviews with, so package it for a busy reader. Put the architecture diagram at the very top of the README and label the batch path, the streaming path, S3, Iceberg, the medallion layers, orchestration, CI/CD, and observability so a hiring manager grasps the whole system in ten seconds. Record a tight 5-8 minute demo: show a batch drop and live Kafka events flowing to bronze, becoming trustworthy silver, rolling up into a gold mart, and lighting up a dashboard, then deliberately break something and show the alert fire and the recovery. Write a short 'design decisions and trade-offs' section (why Iceberg over Delta, why this catalog, why this partitioning, what you would change at 10x scale) because senior engineers are hired on judgment, not just on getting green checkmarks. Include the cost/scale writeup with real numbers, scan-bytes-per-query, monthly dollar estimates, before/after compaction, since cost fluency is rare and memorable. Finally, keep a CHANGELOG or 'lessons learned' note; being able to talk about what broke and how you fixed it is often what lands the offer.
